lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Application Story
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Luiza Sato Eccheli | Lesson 1 -- The Application Story
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect simple and continuous to tell your background

listenings.text: I read exchange applications for six years, and I want to tell you what the committee actually remembers. It is not your score. By the time you reach the interview, everyone in the room has a good score, so the number stops being interesting. What we remember is whether you could explain, in two minutes, why this university and not another one. The strongest candidates did not have the most impressive track record. They had a clear story. Where they were, how long they had been working on something, and where they wanted to go next. And one more thing, because students always worry about it. Nobody on the committee cared about accent. We cared about whether we had to ask you to repeat yourself. If your sentences are clear, your accent is simply part of who you are.

Good afternoon, and thank you for joining this session so early in your degree. Most students come to us six months before the deadline, and that is too late. The application has three parts. First, the language requirement: every partner university asks for an official test, and since the TOEFL moved to a scale from one to six, the most competitive ones expect an overall band of at least four and a half, sometimes five. Second, your grades from the first two years. And third, a short interview, in English, with two members of the committee. Here is my advice. Take a practice test this semester, not next year, so you know exactly how far you are from the cut-off score. Choose three host universities, not one. And remember that a semester abroad is not a vacation. The reading load in a law school is heavy in any language, and you will need to keep up with it from the first week.
